strings.name: Jocelyn Bell Burnell
strings.summary: Born in Northern Ireland, Jocelyn Bell Burnell studied physics at Glasgow and Cambridge. As a doctoral student in 1967, she identified unusual signals in records from a team-built radio telescope and played a key role in discovering pulsars. She did not receive the related 1974 Nobel Prize. She later worked in multiwavelength astronomy, teaching and science communication, and devoted her 2018 Breakthrough Prize money to supporting groups underrepresented in research.
strings.coverageNote: Selected studies, the pulsar discovery, teaching and a 2026 Manchester lecture, checked through November 13, 2026; discovery is described with team contributions acknowledged.
strings.influence.rationale: She participated in discovering pulsars, advanced radio astronomy and science education, and promoted diversity in the research community.

strings.facts.f2.label: Education
strings.facts.f2.value: Physics degree, University of Glasgow; doctorate in radio astronomy, University of Cambridge
strings.highlights.h1.title: Key observations in the pulsar discovery
strings.highlights.h1.text: Identified and investigated unusual radio signals during doctoral research, helping the team establish the first pulsars.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Widening participation in research
strings.highlights.h2.text: Devoted her 2018 Special Breakthrough Prize money to supporting women and other graduate students underrepresented in physics.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Lectured and received a medal in Manchester
strings.timeline.t1.text: Delivered a lecture reflecting on her astronomy career, then received the Dalton Medal from Manchester Lit & Phil.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Received the Copley Medal
strings.timeline.t2.text: Received the Royal Society’s Copley Medal, recognizing her scientific contributions and sustained research influence.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Received a Special Breakthrough Prize and supported research
strings.timeline.t3.text: Received the Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics and directed the $3 million prize toward groups underrepresented in physics.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Became a physics professor at the Open University
strings.timeline.t4.text: After working at several research institutions, became a professor, further combining astronomy research with university teaching.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Excluded from the related Nobel award
strings.timeline.t5.text: The physics prize went to Martin Ryle and Antony Hewish; she was not a recipient, prompting debate over the distribution of scientific recognition.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Completed her Cambridge doctorate
strings.timeline.t6.text: Completed her radio astronomy doctorate, then developed a career in multiwavelength astronomy, teaching and public science communication.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Identified pulsar signals
strings.timeline.t7.text: Found regular pulses while examining paper records from the team’s radio telescope; follow-up investigation helped reveal a new class of object.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Moved from Glasgow to Cambridge
strings.timeline.t8.text: After earning her physics degree, went to Cambridge to study quasars and helped build the radio telescope required for the research.
strings.timeline.t9.title: Born in Northern Ireland
strings.timeline.t9.text: Encountered astronomy through her father as a child; during schooling faced barriers that excluded girls from science classes.
